title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: 10% off promotion
drivers.evidence: Past 10% off promo (2026-03-23) lifted sales x1.6 vs baseline; noise-adjusted uplift from 15 total promotions is x1.15. Model suggests x1.15; adjust to match noise-adjusted evidence.

adjustment.analysis: The 10% off promotion is consistent with past 10% promotions (x1.6 vs baseline in 2026-03-23), but the noise-adjusted uplift is x1.15. The classical model’s 15% uplift is appropriate but slightly optimistic given the recent 10% promo only lifted sales by x1.6 (vs baseline) and the past 15 total promotions average x1.44. The prior week’s Mother’s Day effect was neutral (x1.0 noise-adjusted), so no holiday effect. No evidence of pantry-loading (no dip in the following week after 2026-03-23). The baseline already captures seasonal trend (trend_13=+37.7%). Adjust down from model to reflect noise-adjusted evidence and avoid overfitting.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-04-27 to 2026-05-03 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Promotion: 10% off
  shelf price: 5.76 (-10.1% vs regular price 6.41)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 50.3 | 5%-95%: 22.9 - 77.2 | 10%-90%: 37.8 - 71.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-34% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
